check: Names identify their domain role and behavior; vague placeholders such as `data`, `temp`, `item`, `fn`, `cb`, `handler`, or `x` are not used where a domain-specific name is available. For subscriptions, name the event, listener, and subscription/removal handle by their distinct roles.
why: Generic names hide what a value represents and make it harder to distinguish active subscriptions from callbacks or removal handles.

check: Each learner-authored function does one job; do not treat pre-existing starter scaffolding as the learner's design unless the task asks them to change it. A function that validates, transforms, and formats authored behavior should be split into focused helpers.
why: Mixing validation, business logic, and formatting in one function makes each part harder to test and reuse.

check: Arguments and caller-owned objects or arrays are not mutated unless the spec explicitly requires in-place mutation.
why: Mutating caller inputs causes silent side effects and stale-state bugs elsewhere in the program.

check: Errors are thrown or returned explicitly on invalid input or failure; nothing is swallowed by an empty `catch`. Best-effort cleanup may suppress its own cleanup error when preserving an already-settled result is part of the contract.
why: Swallowing operational errors hides root causes and corrupts downstream state, while cleanup must not accidentally replace an already-settled result.

check: Unexplained numeric or string literals that carry domain meaning or must stay consistent across uses are extracted into named constants; a local defensive bound used once is not automatically a finding.
why: Magic literals obscure business rules and cause drift when the same value must be updated in multiple places.

check: No commented-out code, unreachable branches, unused variables, or leftover `console.log` calls.
why: Dead code clutters the module and misleads readers about which paths are actually executed.

check: No needless cleverness such as nested ternaries or `reduce` where a direct loop or method is clearer. Judge learner-authored changes; pre-existing starter helpers are not a refactoring requirement unless the prompt asks for structural improvement.
why: Over-compressed expressions slow down reading and hide off-by-one or precedence bugs.

check: Promises returned by asynchronous work that the function contract depends on are awaited or otherwise handled, including cleanup in `finally`.
why: Fire-and-forget cleanup can finish after the caller proceeds or leave a rejection unhandled.

check: Subscriptions and other owned callbacks are released when their owner is disposed or unsubscribed; removing a listener prevents the emitter from retaining or invoking that inactive callback.
why: Inactive callbacks retained by long-lived emitters cause memory leaks and can keep disposed consumers reachable.

check: Logic handles the general rule; there is no branch keyed to one specific input value that only exists to make a test pass.
why: A patch for one input hides the real defect, so every other input that hits the same condition is still wrong.

check: Mutable state lives inside the function, closure or instance that owns it, not in module-level variables shared by every caller.
why: Module-level mutable state makes separate callers interfere with each other and makes results depend on call order.
